docs.title: interval
docs.text:
interval(level=0.9, gaussian=False)

Central interval per parameter, (2, p): empirical, or Gaussian from mean and std.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/__init__.py 
def interval(self, level: float = 0.9, gaussian: bool = False) -> np.ndarray:
    """Central interval per parameter, ``(2, p)``: empirical, or Gaussian from mean and std."""
    if gaussian:
        from pinnrl.uq.metrics import _normal_quantile

        z = _normal_quantile(0.5 + level / 2)
        return np.stack([self.mean - z * self.std, self.mean + z * self.std])
    return np.percentile(self.estimates, [50 * (1 - level), 50 * (1 + level)], axis=0)

docs.title: coverage
docs.text:
coverage(lower, upper, truth)

Fraction of intervals [lower, upper] that contain the truth.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/metrics.py 
def coverage(lower: Sequence[float], upper: Sequence[float], truth: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Fraction of intervals ``[lower, upper]`` that contain the truth."""
    lo, hi, t = (np.asarray(v, dtype=float) for v in (lower, upper, truth))
    return float(np.mean((lo <= t) & (t <= hi)))

docs.title: mean_width
docs.text:
mean_width(lower, upper)

Mean width of the intervals.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/metrics.py 
def mean_width(lower: Sequence[float], upper: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Mean width of the intervals."""
    return float(np.mean(np.asarray(upper, dtype=float) - np.asarray(lower, dtype=float)))

docs.title: gaussian_interval
docs.text:
gaussian_interval(mean, std, level=0.9)

Central interval of a Gaussian at the given level.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/metrics.py 
def gaussian_interval(mean: float, std: float, level: float = 0.9) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Central interval of a Gaussian at the given level."""
    z = _normal_quantile(0.5 + level / 2)
    return mean - z * std, mean + z * std

docs.title: sample_interval
docs.text:
sample_interval(samples, level=0.9)

Central empirical interval of a set of samples at the given level.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/metrics.py 
def sample_interval(samples: Sequence[float], level: float = 0.9) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Central empirical interval of a set of samples at the given level."""
    s = np.asarray(samples, dtype=float)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(s, [50 * (1 - level), 50 * (1 + level)])
    return float(lo), float(hi)

docs.title: crps_gaussian
docs.text:
crps_gaussian(mean, std, truth)

Continuous ranked probability score of a Gaussian forecast (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007).

CRPS = sigma [ z (2 Phi(z) - 1) + 2 phi(z) - 1/sqrt(pi) ] with z = (y - mu) / sigma. Lower is better; it rewards both calibration and sharpness.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/metrics.py 
def crps_gaussian(mean: float, std: float, truth: float) -> float:
    """Continuous ranked probability score of a Gaussian forecast (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007).

    ``CRPS = sigma [ z (2 Phi(z) - 1) + 2 phi(z) - 1/sqrt(pi) ]`` with ``z = (y - mu) / sigma``.
    Lower is better; it rewards both calibration and sharpness.
    """
    if std <= 0:
        return abs(truth - mean)
    z = (truth - mean) / std
    phi = math.exp(-0.5 * z * z) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
    Phi = 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(z / math.sqrt(2)))
    return std * (z * (2 * Phi - 1) + 2 * phi - 1 / math.sqrt(math.pi))

docs.title: crps_samples
docs.text:
crps_samples(samples, truth)

CRPS of an empirical forecast: E|X - y| - E|X - X'| / 2.

Source code in pinnrl/uq/metrics.py 
def crps_samples(samples: Sequence[float], truth: float) -> float:
    """CRPS of an empirical forecast: ``E|X - y| - E|X - X'| / 2``."""
    s = np.asarray(samples, dtype=float)
    term1 = float(np.mean(np.abs(s - truth)))
    term2 = float(np.mean(np.abs(s[:, None] - s[None, :])))
    return term1 - 0.5 * term2

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The point of pinnrl is to estimate unknown physics from measurements and to say how far the estimate can be trusted. That claim rests on conditions, and the pages here state them. Each module of the inverse-modelling core cites the condition it relies on, so that a number the package reports comes with the assumption that makes it meaningful.

Page Question it answers Used by Well-posedness and stability When does a small change in the data give a small change in the estimate, and what does the physics do to an ill-posed problem? the disturbance suite, the stability constants Identifiability and conditioning Can the sensors determine the parameters at all, and which combinations do they determine badly? pinnrl.analysis, experiments F01–F05 and K01 The Bayesian view and uncertainty Why is the PINN loss a negative log-posterior, what does that make the loss weights, and what counts as a calibrated error bar? pinnrl.uq, K39, F06, K10 The numerical-analysis bridge What do consistency, stability and convergence mean for a PINN, and how does its error relate to the training residual? the error estimates, K06–K08 Equivalence regions and swarm sampling Why report the set of parameters that fit the data rather than one estimate, and how to sample it when the problem is nonlinear? pinnrl.uq, K10, K45–K48

The pages are short on purpose. They give the statement, the condition, the consequence for a PINN, and the reference where the proof lives. The notation is shared: \(u\) is the state, \(\theta\) the parameters to identify, \(\mathcal{N}_\theta[u] = 0\) the governing equation, \(y = \mathcal{H}u + \varepsilon\) the observations through a sensor operator \(\mathcal{H}\) with noise \(\varepsilon\), and \(u_w\) the network with weights \(w\).

Reference papers

The maintainer's reference papers on nonlinear uncertainty (the Oviedo particle-swarm work on sampling equivalence regions) are summarized in Equivalence regions and swarm sampling and cited by DOI. The PDFs stay out of the repository.

docs.title: The loss is a negative log-posterior
docs.text:
Take Gaussian observation noise, \(y_i = (\mathcal{H}u)_i + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_i^2)\), and a Gaussian belief that the residual, the boundary and the initial mismatch are zero with scales \(\sigma_r\), \(\sigma_b\), \(\sigma_0\). Up to a constant, minus the log of the posterior over \((w, \theta)\) is

\[ -\log p(w, \theta \mid y) = \frac{1}{2\sigma_r^2}\|\mathcal{N}_\theta[u_w]\|^2 + \frac{1}{2\sigma_b^2}\|\mathcal{B}u_w\|^2 + \frac{1}{2\sigma_0^2}\|u_w(\cdot, 0) - u_0\|^2 + \sum_i \frac{(y_i - (\mathcal{H}u_w)_i)^2}{2\sigma_i^2} - \log p(w, \theta). \]

This is the PINN loss, with weights \(1/\sigma^2\) (Kaipio & Somersalo, 2005; Stuart, 2010). Training finds the maximum-a-posteriori point, and the weights are not tuning knobs: the data weight is the inverse noise variance, and the physics weights encode how much model error one admits. Experiment K39 tests whether setting the data weight from the measured noise beats tuned weights, which F01 motivates: a fixed weight that ignores the noise level biased the estimate at few, noisy points.

Two things follow for pinnrl. A per-sensor noise level is a per-observation weight, which fisher_information already accepts. And a change of weights is a change of prior, so results obtained with different weights are not comparable without saying so.

docs.title: Sources of uncertainty
docs.text:
An error bar on \(\theta\) must say which of these it covers.

Source Where it comes from How it shows Aleatoric measurement noise \(\varepsilon\) the spread across noise draws; bounded below by \(F^{-1}\) Parametric epistemic finite data, correlated parameters the posterior width along sloppy directions Surrogate the network's approximation error and the non-convex training the bias of F01, the seed spread Model form the equation is not the process a residual structure the surrogate cannot remove (F08) Input a recorded input with an offset (a steam temperature) a shift of the estimate along the direction the input can be traded against; ignored, the interval is too narrow (J06)

The Fisher bound covers the first. Ensembles over seeds and over noise draws separate the first from the third. Model-form error is the one that no method internal to the model detects, and it is why a twin must report its residual against the plant.

docs.title: Approximating the posterior
docs.text:
• Laplace. Expand the loss to second order at the optimum; the posterior is Gaussian with covariance the inverse Hessian (MacKay, 1992). The block for \(\theta\), after eliminating \(w\), is the generalized Gauss–Newton approximation of \(F^{-1}\). It reuses the sensitivities of identifiability, which is why the conditioning module comes first on the roadmap. Experiment K41 asks how much of the network the Hessian must cover.
  • Deep ensembles. Retrain from several initializations and treat the estimates as posterior samples (Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel & Blundell, 2017). The spread captures the surrogate's non-convexity, which Laplace does not, and misses nothing that retraining reveals. Experiments F06 and K40 measure coverage against the ensemble size.
  • Sampling. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo over \((w, \theta)\) (Yang, Meng & Karniadakis, 2021) is the reference posterior for small networks (K42) and too costly for the rest.
  • Conformal intervals. Hold out sensors, calibrate the residual quantile on them, and get finite-sample coverage with no distributional assumption (Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer, 2005). It bounds the field prediction rather than \(\theta\) (K44).

A broad comparison of these on physics-informed models is Psaros et al. (2023).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
An interval is calibrated when it contains the truth as often as it claims: a 90 % interval, over many data sets, should cover 90 % of the time. Coverage alone is not enough, since an interval that is always the whole real line is calibrated. The quantities pinnrl reports, from F06 and K10 onward, are:

  • empirical coverage of the nominal interval across synthetic data sets with known truth;
  • width, the sharpness, which should be as small as coverage allows (Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery, 2007);
  • the continuous ranked probability score, a proper scoring rule that rewards both at once (Gneiting & Raftery, 2007).

A method is kept only where it is calibrated, and the page of each method states the regime in which that was checked.

Experiment J06 measures, on the evaporator, the conditions under which the Fisher (Laplace) interval of an identified function is calibrated, and each is an assumption the interval inherits rather than something the data check for it:

  • the form assumed for the unknown contains the truth. A ramp assumed for a fouling curve that saturates gives a ±2.5 % interval around an estimate 25 % off. The form sets the width as much as the data do (±2 % for a ramp, ±8 % for six modes, on the same records), and only the misfit says when it is wrong;
  • the model's own error is below the interval's width. A lumped model biased by 2.7 % supports a ±7 % interval and not a ±2 % one;
  • every input the unknown can be traded against is either measured to that accuracy or among the unknowns with its prior. A steam record trusted to 0.3 K and taken at face value reduces coverage to 21–52 %; estimated under its prior, coverage returns at five times the width, and that width is the honest one.

An interval reported for a process estimate should name the three: the form, the model, and the inputs it conditions on.

docs.title: Nonlinear uncertainty: equivalence regions and swarm sampling
docs.text: The Fisher bound and the Laplace approximation of the Bayesian view are linear statements: they describe the posterior by an ellipse around one estimate. A body of work on geophysical inverse problems by Fernández-Martínez, García-Gonzalo and co-workers (University of Oviedo) argues that the object to report is not the estimate but the region of equivalence, the set of all parameters that fit the data within the noise, and that this region is sampled rather than linearized. This page summarizes the nine papers that make that case and what they change in the design of pinnrl.uq.

docs.title: The region of equivalence
docs.text:
With a forward map \(F\), observations \(d_{\text{obs}} = F(m_{\text{true}}) + \delta d\) and a tolerance \(\mathrm{tol}\) set by the noise, the solution of an inverse problem is the set

\[ M_{\mathrm{tol}} = \{\, m : \|F(m) - d_{\text{obs}}\| \le \mathrm{tol} \,\}, \]

not its minimum-misfit member (Pallero et al., 2018, after Tarantola). Three facts about it carry over to PINN identification unchanged:

  1. The best-fit point is not the truth. With noise, the minimizer \(m_0\) of the perturbed misfit satisfies \(\nabla c(m_0) = 2 J^\top \delta d \ne 0\) for the noise-free misfit \(c\): the true model lies inside \(M_{\mathrm{tol}}\) with a higher misfit than the best fit. Reporting the minimizer alone reports the noise.
  2. The linearized region is only local. The ellipse from the Jacobian at \(m_0\) (the Fisher ellipse of identifiability) matches \(M_{\mathrm{tol}}\) near \(m_0\) and nowhere else; for nonlinear forward maps the true region is a curved valley (the "banana") elongated along the small singular values of \(J\), possibly disconnected, and the ellipse both includes models outside it and misses models inside it. F02 is such a case in pinnrl: the PINN's optimum for the two KdV coefficients sits 20 % from the truth with a tight Fisher ellipse around it.
  3. Noise and regularization deform the region. Noise shrinks the low-misfit part of the valley and may move the best fit into a different basin (Fernández-Martínez et al., 2014a, b); a Tikhonov term bounds the region anisotropically, most along the directions of highest uncertainty, and can create local minima. For a PINN the physics weights play the role of the regularization: F07 found that the soft physics term flattens the data-misfit profile 2.5–12×, which is the same deformation seen from inside the loss.

docs.title: Sampling while optimizing
docs.text:
The Oviedo group samples \(M_{\mathrm{tol}}\) with particle swarms used in their exploratory form: a swarm of parameter vectors moves under

\[ v_i^{k+1} = \omega\, v_i^k + \phi_1 (g^k - x_i^k) + \phi_2 (l_i^k - x_i^k), \qquad x_i^{k+1} = x_i^k + v_i^{k+1}, \]

with \(g^k\) the best position of the swarm, \(l_i^k\) the best of particle \(i\), \(\phi_1, \phi_2\) random accelerations and \(\omega\) the inertia; every evaluated position with misfit below the tolerance is kept as a sample. The method needs only forward solves (no gradient, no inverse operator, no regularization or reference model), and its exploration is controlled by one theory:

  • PSO is a damped mass–spring system. Each particle obeys the stochastic second-order difference equation \(x^{k+1} + (\phi - \omega - 1) x^k + \omega x^{k-1} = \phi_1 g^k + \phi_2 l^k\), the discretization of \(x'' + (1 - \omega) x' + \phi (x - o) = 0\) with a stochastic centre of attraction \(o\) (Fernández-Martínez & García-Gonzalo, 2008, 2011). The generalized PSO uses a time step \(\Delta t \ne 1\): larger steps explore, smaller steps freeze the swarm.
  • A family from the discretization. Centering or delaying the velocity and acceleration differences gives CC-PSO, CP-PSO, PP-PSO and RR-PSO (Fernández-Martínez & García-Gonzalo, 2009, 2012; García-Gonzalo et al., 2014). All are linearly isomorphic for the same delay; they differ in convergence rate and exploration. CC-PSO and PSO converge fastest; CP-PSO and PP-PSO are the most exploratory and the recommended samplers; RR-PSO performs best on benchmarks with its good parameters on the line \(\phi = 3(\omega - 3/2)\).
  • Stability regions replace tuning. The mean trajectory is stable for \(|\omega| < 1\), \(0 < \bar\phi < 2(\omega + 1)\); the variance has its own, smaller region, whose upper border (the USL curve) is given analytically for any distribution of \((\omega, \phi_1, \phi_2)\) with finite first moments (García-Gonzalo & Fernández-Martínez, 2014). Good parameters lie just inside that border, where the variance is large and successive positions are uncorrelated: high variance and temporal uncorrelation improve exploration of ill-posed problems (2008). "Cloud" versions give every particle its own parameters drawn near the border, and its own time step, so nothing is tuned by hand. The history and the plea for uniformisation (García-Gonzalo & Fernández-Martínez, 2012; Fernández-Martínez & García-Gonzalo, 2013) argue that most published PSO variants are unnecessary once the stability analysis is understood.
  • Collapse is the failure mode. The swarm's dispersion, the median distance of the particles to their centre of gravity relative to its initial value, is monitored every iteration; when it collapses the sampling stops, exploration is raised (larger \(\Delta t\), repulsive forces), or the collapsed particles are counted as one sample. The sampled set is an approximation of the posterior, not a posterior sample: whether and when PSO performs importance sampling is stated as the open question (2013).
  • Posterior statistics by counting. From the retained samples: min–max ranges per parameter, a mean or median model with its interquartile range, percentiles and empirical CDFs of any derived quantity, and histograms that reveal multimodality (Pallero et al., 2018, on a 300-parameter gravity inversion with 40,000 forward solves and 25,429 retained models).
  • Model reduction before sampling. An isotropic search space cannot be sampled efficiently beyond about ten dimensions, so field-valued unknowns are expanded in a reduced basis (principal components of prior scenarios, or the singular vectors of a model already in the low-misfit region, plus one high-frequency term) and the swarm moves in the coefficients (Pallero et al., 2018; Fernández-Martínez, 2015).

docs.title: What this changes in pinnrl.uq
docs.text:
The roadmap's UQ module was planned as a likelihood-based data term, deep ensembles, a Laplace approximation and calibration metrics. The equivalence-region view adds four things and sharpens two.

  1. Report regions, not points. The primary output of an identification is the set of parameter values whose misfit is within the noise tolerance, \(\mathrm{tol}^2 = (1 + \varepsilon)\, N \sigma^2\) for Gaussian noise, with the point estimate as one member. Intervals, percentiles and CDFs are derived from the set by counting. The Fisher ellipse and the Laplace Gaussian are reported next to it as the linear approximation, so the two can disagree visibly (the F02 case).
  2. A swarm sampler over the parameters. For \(p \lesssim 10\) parameters a cloud CP-PSO over \(\theta\) is the sampler: each particle's parameters drawn inside the second-order stability border, dispersion monitored, collapse handled. It needs a cheap forward map for each \(\theta\), which is the real design question for a PINN, where a forward solve is a training run. Two routes: a parametric surrogate \(u_w(x, t;\, \theta)\) with \(\theta\) as a network input, trained once over the prior range and evaluated in microseconds (the forward emulator the swarm needs), or warm-started retraining, a few hundred steps from the nearest particle's weights (the F07 profile, generalized to \(p\) dimensions and to a moving swarm). The parametric surrogate is the one to build first; the KdV pair and the Burgers viscosity are its test cases, since their regions are known to be displaced from the truth.
  3. A tolerance from the noise model, and the physics weight as regularization. The tolerance is set by \(\sigma\) (K39), and the dependence of the region on the physics weight is measured and documented, since it plays the role Tikhonov's term plays in the papers: too strong, and the region shrinks anisotropically toward what the surrogate can represent; too weak, and the data are fitted by a field that violates the equation.
  4. Reduced bases for fields. When the unknown is a coefficient field or a closure (roadmap v0.6), it is parametrized by fewer than ten modes (principal components of prior scenarios, or Karhunen–Loève modes) and the swarm samples the coefficients. This is also the bridge to the measurement-design work: the modes the data do not constrain are the ones a new sensor should.
  5. Ensembles are a swarm without dynamics. Deep ensembles over seeds are a crude sample of \(M_{\mathrm{tol}}\); the papers' dispersion diagnostic and the "collapsed particles count once" rule apply to them. K10 compares ensembles, the Laplace ellipse, the swarm sample and a reference posterior (K42) by coverage; the open question of when a swarm sample is a posterior sample is answered empirically there, by weighting retained samples with \(\exp(-\text{misfit}/2\sigma^2)\) and checking coverage against HMC.
  6. Optimizer stability from the same mathematics. The second-order (variance) stability regions of a stochastically forced damped oscillator are the same analysis that sets a safe step for a momentum optimizer under gradient noise. D01/D02 can use it to choose the learning rate and momentum from the Hessian spectrum of K03 rather than by trial.

Backlog entries K45–K48 carry these items; the roadmap's item 5 lists the swarm sampler and the parametric surrogate next to the Laplace approximation.

docs.title: Structural identifiability
docs.text:
Parameters are structurally identifiable when the noise-free observations determine them uniquely: \(\mathcal{H}u_{\theta_1} = \mathcal{H}u_{\theta_2}\) on the sensor set implies \(\theta_1 = \theta_2\) (Bellman & Åström, 1970). It is a property of the equation, the sensor operator and the experiment, not of the data quality. Two parameters that only ever appear as a product are not structurally identifiable from any amount of data; a rate that only acts in a regime the sensors never see is not identifiable either.

For small models, structural identifiability is decided symbolically (Chiş, Banga & Balsa-Canto, 2011): the observations are differentiated with respect to time and the resulting algebraic relations are solved for \(\theta\). Experiment K11 does this with SymPy for the catalogue entries that have a closed form.

docs.title: Practical identifiability
docs.text:
Identifiable in principle is not identifiable in practice. With noise \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)\), the information the observations carry about \(\theta\) near the truth is the Fisher matrix

\[ F = J^\top \Sigma^{-1} J, \qquad J_{ij} = \frac{\partial (\mathcal{H}u_\theta)_i}{\partial \theta_j}, \]

and the Cramér–Rao inequality bounds the covariance of any unbiased estimator from below by \(F^{-1}\) (Cramér, 1946). Its diagonal gives the smallest standard deviation each parameter can have; its correlations say which parameters the data confuse. A parameter is practically identifiable when its bound is small compared with the parameter itself, for the sensors and the noise one actually has (Raue et al., 2009; Wieland et al., 2021).

pinnrl.analysis.closed_form_bound computes \(J\) by symbolic differentiation of a closed-form solution and returns \(F\), \(F^{-1}\), the standard deviations, the correlation matrix and the eigen-decomposition. For the heat diffusivity, \(\partial u/\partial\alpha = -\pi^2 t\, u\): the information sits at late times and mid-domain, and a probe at \(x = 0.5\) carries more of it than one near the wall. F01 found the spread of the PINN estimate across noise draws to match this bound to about 20 % once the noise dominated the surrogate's own error.

docs.title: Sloppy directions and conditioning
docs.text:
The eigenvectors of \(F\) are parameter combinations; the eigenvalues say how well the data determine each. A spectrum spanning many decades, with a few stiff directions and many sloppy ones, is the rule rather than the exception in models with several parameters (Gutenkunst et al., 2007). The condition number \(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) of \(F\) is then the first diagnostic to report: it tells how much a relative error in the data can grow into a relative error along the sloppiest direction. Experiment F02 measures it for the two KdV coefficients, whose amplitude and width enter through \(3/\alpha\) and \(\sqrt{\beta}\) and are therefore correlated by the data.

Two different conditionings appear in a PINN inverse problem and should not be confused:

  • the conditioning of the inverse problem, from \(F\), which no solver can improve without new sensors or a prior;
  • the conditioning of training, from the loss Hessian or the neural tangent kernel, which the differential operator drives (high-order derivatives stiffen it) and which optimizers and preconditioning can improve (Wang, Teng & Perdikaris, 2021; Wang, Yu & Perdikaris, 2022).

Roadmap item 3 computes both; the second is the subject of experiments K03 and K04.

docs.title: Profile likelihood
docs.text: The Fisher bound is local. When the posterior is far from Gaussian, or when a direction is nearly flat, the profile likelihood is the honest check (Raue et al., 2009): fix one parameter on a grid of values, re-optimize everything else, and plot the minimal loss against the fixed value. A flat profile means the parameter is not practically identifiable; an asymmetric one means the Gaussian error bar is wrong on one side. Experiment F07 does this by retraining the PINN at each grid value.

docs.title: Sensitivities without a closed form
docs.text:
Most problems of interest have no closed-form solution, and the surrogate's output does not depend on \(\theta\) directly: the parameters enter through the residual. Three routes to \(J\) remain, in order of cost.

  1. Finite differences of a numerical reference, when one exists: F03 does this for Burgers with the Cole–Hopf solution at \(\nu(1 \pm 1\,\%)\).
  2. The implicit-function theorem at the trained optimum: \(\partial u_w/\partial\theta = -H_{ww}^{-1} H_{w\theta}\) with \(H\) the loss Hessian, computed with Hessian-vector products. This is experiment K01, and it also yields the Laplace approximation of the Bayesian view.
  3. Retraining at perturbed \(\theta\), the brute-force check of the other two.

Each is validated against the exact layer on a catalogue entry with a closed form before it is trusted elsewhere.

docs.title: Field-valued unknowns
docs.text:
When the unknown is a function, \(\alpha(x)\) or \(\alpha(t)\), the parameter space is infinite-dimensional and the questions above are asked of its modes. For the heat equation in conservative form, \(u_t = (\alpha(x) u_x)_x\), the first-order response of the solution to a perturbation \(\delta\alpha\) solves \(\delta u_t = (\alpha\, \delta u_x)_x + (\delta\alpha\, u_x)_x\): the perturbation acts through the flux \(\delta\alpha\, u_x\), so \(\alpha\) is invisible wherever \(u_x\) vanishes, and a localized \(\delta\alpha\) is diffused before it reaches the sensors. Modes of \(\alpha\) that are oscillatory, or supported where the gradient is small, lie in the sloppy directions of the (now infinite) Fisher matrix. A time-varying \(\alpha(t)\) is better placed: it changes the decay rate of every mode at once, and \(\int_0^t \alpha\) is read directly from the amplitude of the solution.

The practical test is the one of the previous section with the function in place of the parameter: compare the solution for the true field with the one for the best constant (or the best low-order polynomial). If the two differ by about the surrogate's own field error or less, the PINN cannot distinguish them and the recovered field will collapse to that constant, however expressive the network, even when the Fisher information of the data (with an exact forward model) says the modes are determined: the forward error, not the sensors, is the limit, and the remedy is forward accuracy. Experiment F09 shows both outcomes on heat: a two-layer \(\alpha(x)\) whose solution is 20 % away from any constant is recovered in shape; a centred bump whose solution a constant reproduces to 4 % is not. A smooth network also turns a jump in \(\alpha(t)\) into a ramp, the finite resolution of a surrogate with a few hundred weights. Reduced bases for the field (K48) and pointwise intervals (K47) are the next steps.

docs.title: Consistency, stability, convergence
docs.text:
For a linear well-posed evolution problem, a consistent discretization converges if and only if it is stable (Lax & Richtmyer, 1956). Consistency says the scheme's residual on the exact solution vanishes with the mesh; stability says the discrete solution operator is bounded uniformly in the mesh; convergence follows with the bound as the constant:

\[ \|u - u_h\| \le C_{\text{stab}}\, \|\text{residual of } u_h\|. \]

For explicit time-stepping, stability is the CFL condition (Courant, Friedrichs & Lewy, 1928): the explicit heat scheme in pinnrl-benchmark fdm needs \(\alpha\,\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2\), and von Neumann analysis gives the same number by asking that no Fourier mode grow. For nonlinear problems the role of the stability operator is played by an energy estimate, a bound on a norm of the solution that the equation preserves or decreases.

docs.title: The same statement for a PINN
docs.text:
A PINN has no mesh, but the structure survives. Mishra & Molinaro (2022) prove, for a class of forward problems, an estimate of the form

\[ \|u - u_w\| \;\le\; C_{\text{stab}}\,\big(\,\mathcal{E}_{\text{train}} + \mathcal{E}_{\text{quad}}\,\big), \]

with \(\mathcal{E}_{\text{train}}\) the residual and boundary mismatch on the collocation points (what training minimizes), \(\mathcal{E}_{\text{quad}}\) the quadrature error of replacing the integral of the residual by a sample mean, and \(C_{\text{stab}}\) the conditional-stability constant of the PDE. A companion result covers a class of inverse problems (Mishra & Molinaro, 2022b), with the data misfit added to the right-hand side and the stability constant now that of the inverse problem, the modulus \(\omega\) of well-posedness. De Ryck & Mishra (2024) survey the estimates; Shin, Darbon & Karniadakis (2020) give the convergence statement for linear second-order equations.

Three things the package can measure follow.

  1. The training residual is not the error. The ratio of the two is an estimate of \(C_{\text{stab}}\). Experiments K06 and K07 record it across the catalogue, and compare it with the constants the conditional-stability theory gives where one is known. A constant in the hundreds for Allen–Cahn, and near one for the heat equation, would explain the B01 finding that the Allen–Cahn error stayed above 0.5 for every sampler at a small residual.
  2. Quadrature error scales with dimension. A Monte Carlo sample mean of \(N\) points has error \(\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\) in any dimension, but the constant grows with the variance of the residual over the domain, and the residual of a trained network is rough. In five dimensions the gallery of custom equations needed four times the points for a worse result than in one, which is the quadrature term at work. Experiment K08 sweeps the dimension and reports both terms separately.
  3. Causality. Time-marching schemes respect the direction of information; a PINN trained on all of space-time at once does not, and can settle on a wrong solution that has a small residual (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021). The metastable Allen–Cahn solution of B01 is such a case. Causal weighting and time-marching (H03, H04) are the PINN equivalents of marching in time.

docs.title: Linearized stability of coupled systems
docs.text: For a system \(u_t = f(u; \theta)\) (the ODE entries, the reaction terms of Gray–Scott or the Brusselator, a process model with several balances), the Jacobian \(\partial f/\partial u\) at an operating point gives the linearized dynamics. Its eigenvalues decide whether perturbations decay, and their ratio is the stiffness, which bounds the time step of an explicit method and stiffens the PINN loss in the same way a high-order derivative does. Experiment K09 computes the spectrum for the catalogue systems and for the evaporator model. Two cautions from it: the discretised transport operator of a process model is non-normal (an upwind scheme has one defective eigenvalue \(-v/\Delta z\)), so its computed spectrum is a pseudospectrum and the stiffness it suggests is the grid's, which a PINN never sees; and on ODEs the PINN's failures were trivial solutions close to the initial condition (pendulum, SIR, Lorenz), not the stiff systems. The process twins report the physical rates (residence, source) and the number of fast units in the window instead.

docs.title: High dimensions
docs.text: Both constants degrade with dimension: the quadrature constant through the variance of the residual, and the stability constant through the growth of the domain's boundary relative to its interior. Experiment K08 and paper P12 measure how. The maintainer's rule, applied to every system with many state variables, is to report the spectrum of the linearized dynamics and the two error terms before trusting a surrogate in that dimension.

docs.title: Hadamard's three conditions
docs.text:
A problem is well posed when a solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data (Hadamard, 1902). Forward problems for the equations in the catalogue are well posed on their domains: given \(\theta\), the initial and boundary data determine \(u\), and nearby data give nearby solutions.

Inverse problems are usually not. Recovering \(\theta\) (or an initial state, or a coefficient field) from \(y = \mathcal{H}u_\theta + \varepsilon\) inverts a map that smooths. Diffusion damps the mode \(\sin k\pi x\) by \(e^{-\alpha k^2 \pi^2 t}\), so reading the initial state from a late measurement amplifies noise at mode \(k\) by \(e^{\alpha k^2 \pi^2 t}\): continuity fails. Uniqueness can also fail, which is the subject of identifiability.

docs.title: Conditional stability
docs.text:
Ill-posedness is rarely total. Restrict the unknown to a set where it is bounded in a stronger norm (an a-priori bound \(\|\theta\|_{Z} \le M\)) and continuity returns, but with a modulus that is not Lipschitz:

\[ \|\theta_1 - \theta_2\|_X \le \omega\big(\|y_1 - y_2\|_Y\big), \qquad \omega(\delta) \to 0 \text{ as } \delta \to 0, \]

with \(\omega\) a power \(\delta^\mu\) in the good cases (Hölder stability) and a logarithm \(|\log\delta|^{-\mu}\) in the bad ones, such as the backward heat problem or the Cauchy problem for elliptic equations (Alessandrini et al., 2009; Isakov, 2017). The exponent tells how many digits of the data survive into the estimate: with Hölder exponent \(\mu = 1/2\), four digits of data give two digits of parameter.

A scalar parameter in an otherwise known equation is the benign case. For the heat diffusivity, F01 found the spread of the estimate across noise draws to follow the Cramér–Rao bound, so the map from data to \(\alpha\) is locally Lipschitz with a constant the Fisher information gives; see identifiability.

docs.title: Regularization, and the physics as a regularizer
docs.text:
Classical inverse theory restores continuity by regularization: minimize a data misfit plus a penalty that encodes the a-priori bound, \(\|\mathcal{H}u_\theta - y\|^2 + \lambda R(\theta)\), and choose \(\lambda\) from the noise level (Engl, Hanke & Neubauer, 1996). The penalty selects, among the many \(\theta\) that fit the data equally, the one the prior prefers.

A PINN inverse problem has the same shape, with two differences. The residual term \(\|\mathcal{N}_\theta[u_w]\|^2\) regularizes the state: the network cannot fit noise with a function that violates the equation. And the parameter \(\theta\) carries no explicit penalty, so it is regularized only through the physics. This is why the fixed data weight of F01 produced a bias at few, noisy points: the residual term preferred a smoother field, and the smoother field implied slower diffusion. The Bayesian view turns the weights into noise levels, which is the principled way to set \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Stability of the estimate under disturbances
docs.text:
For a disturbance \(\delta y\) of the data, the first-order response of a least-squares estimate is

\[ \delta\theta \approx (J^\top \Sigma^{-1} J)^{-1} J^\top \Sigma^{-1}\, \delta y, \qquad J = \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}u_\theta}{\partial\theta}, \]

so the Fisher information \(F = J^\top\Sigma^{-1}J\) is both the covariance of random errors and the gain on systematic ones (bias, drift, a stuck sensor). The disturbance suite of the roadmap (item 4, experiments K05–K07) measures the observed \(\delta\theta\) against this prediction for noise, bias, dropout and delay, and for perturbations of the initial and boundary data; the ratio is an empirical stability constant.

docs.title: What a PINN adds and what it does not
docs.text:
The network introduces its own failure to depend continuously on the data: training is non-convex, and the surrogate reaches a residual that is small but not zero. Two consequences matter for an estimate.

  • The surrogate's approximation error is absorbed by the parameters. F01 measured this as a bias of about 2 % that no number of observations removes.
  • Different seeds, same data, can give different estimates when the problem is ill-conditioned. The seed spread is therefore reported next to the noise spread, and F04 checks that the estimate does not depend on where it started.

Neither is a property of the inverse problem; both are properties of the solver, and the numerical-analysis bridge treats them as such.
